sections.html:
Heber Valley, a basin ringed by mountains on the Wasatch Back, is the heart of Wasatch County in north central Utah. Heber City serves as seat and biggest city. Midway is here too, along with a piece of Park City. Neighbors are Salt Lake, Summit, Duchesne and Utah counties, and over half the land lies above 7,500 feet.

The population was 8,523 in 1980, 34,788 in 2020 and about 38,514 in the 2025 estimate, and the 2020 count was 47.8% above the 2010 count. About 76.3% of households own their home. Heber City, 43 miles southeast of Salt Lake City at 5,601 feet, had 16,856 residents in 2020, and about 27% of them commute to Park City or Salt Lake City. Midway had 6,003 residents. Some Midway subdivisions require a share of Swiss-style features on new houses, so ask about design rules if you inherit or list a home there.

Long, snowy winters mean buyers look first at the roof, the furnace and exposed pipes. Heber City gets about 75 inches of snow a year over roughly 29 snowy days, with January and December the heaviest months at 21.5 and 17.8 inches. The average January high is 36.5 degrees and the average January low is 12.5, the record low is minus 38, and the average July high is near 89.5.

Snow is not a flaw. Still, an inspector can easily spot postponed roof, gutter or heating work on an older Heber Valley house. If the house needs that work and you would rather not pay for it first, an as-is cash purchase is a common answer.

sections.h2: Who runs property tax in Wasatch County
sections.html:
Three offices split the work. The assessor sets values, the clerk/auditor calculates rates and handles value appeals, and the treasurer collects payment. The county council doubles as the Board of Equalization that rules on those appeals.

Utah taxes property at 100% of fair market value as of January 1. If you occupy the home for 183 or more consecutive days in the year, a 45% primary residence exemption applies. Farmland that qualifies can be valued by what it produces, with greenbelt applications due May 1. Before a taxing entity can raise the revenue it collects, it has to hold a public hearing, and individual rates shift when county-wide values shift. The county's property tax system page explains the system in full.

Valuation happens January 1 and the cycle ends with tax hearings in December.

DateEvent
January 1Valuation date
January 31Urban farming renewals due
May 1Greenbelt applications due
May 22Real property assessment roll closes
July 22Valuation notices mailed by the clerk/auditor
August 1 to September 15Board of Equalization takes value appeals
October 30Tax notices mailed by the treasurer
November 30Payment due
December 1 to 31Hearings on tax increases for calendar-budget entities

Read the July valuation notice closely each year, since it is your first look at the new value. If the number looks wrong, the appeal window runs from August 1 to September 15, so do not let the notice sit in a pile of mail. A seller who appeals before listing may also give buyers a lower, better supported tax figure.

Mail a payment postmarked on or before November 30 and there is no penalty. The treasurer accepts online payment through Instant Payments but no credit cards.

  • A payment received between December 1 and January 31 draws a 1% penalty.
  • A payment postmarked after January 31 draws a 2.5% penalty plus interest back to January 1.
  • Make checks out to Wasatch County Treasurer, mail them to 25 N. Main, Heber City, UT 84032, and write the parcel number on the check.

Walk-in hours are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, and the main line is (435) 657-3218. Ask your mortgage company whether it pays the tax for you. People often lose track of that after a refinance or a sale of the loan.

An updated list of multiyear delinquent accounts goes up on the county site every week. Interest accrues all the time, so a payoff figure changes daily. For the exact number, call (435) 657-3217.

Get your appeal to the clerk/auditor by 5 p.m. on September 15. You can file online or at 25 North Main Street in Heber City. The state rule is the later of September 15 or 45 days after notice from the county, and the county board then has 60 days to decide.

Attach proof. The county denies any application that lacks evidence of your own value estimate. Parcels can be combined in one appeal when the owner is the same and they lie in the same general area, though every parcel needs its own supporting evidence. You can reach the clerk/auditor at (435) 657-3190.

When the board's decision goes against you, the Utah State Tax Commission hears a further appeal. File Form TC-194 with the county auditor within 30 days of the county's decision. The governing statute is Utah Code 59-2-1004.

sections.h2: Taxes when you sell a Wasatch County house
sections.html:
Request the payoff from the treasurer before you sign anything, and compare it with the closing statement. The weekly delinquent listing is the fastest way to see whether your parcel is on it.

  • Pull your latest tax notice and the July valuation notice.
  • Ask the mortgage servicer if an escrow account already covered this year.
  • Call (435) 657-3217 on the day you plan to close and get the current payoff.
  • For an empty house or seasonal home, update the mailing address so notices find you.

Back taxes, deferred repairs or the cost of carrying a second home are common reasons people want out. We buy houses in Wasatch County as-is and can work around all of them. Any tax balance comes out of your proceeds at closing, so you need no cash up front, and you can read the payoff figure before agreeing to a sale.

A cash sale also removes the usual list of listing chores: no showings, no staging, and no waiting on a buyer's lender. You pick the closing date, and the title company handles the tax split and the deed.

faqs.q: How much is Wasatch County property tax due and when?
faqs.a: The due date is November 30, and anything postmarked by then is penalty-free. Tax notices are mailed on October 30. The amount depends on your assessed value and the combined rate of every taxing entity that covers your address.

faqs.q: Does Wasatch County give a break for a primary residence?
faqs.a: Yes. Utah applies a 45% exemption to a home you occupy for 183 or more consecutive days in a year. Send residential exemption forms to the Assessor's Office before June.

faqs.q: When is the deadline to appeal my Wasatch County property value?
faqs.a: The county board accepts appeals from August 1 through September 15 at 5 p.m. Evidence of your own value estimate has to arrive with the form. File online or at the clerk/auditor's office at 25 North Main Street in Heber City.

faqs.q: Can I pay Wasatch County property tax by credit card?
faqs.a: No. You can pay online through Instant Payments, mail a check to 25 N. Main, Heber City, or visit the office on a weekday between 8:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Wasatch County house if the taxes are unpaid?
faqs.a: In most cases, yes. Get the payoff amount from the treasurer at (435) 657-3217, and pay it from the proceeds at closing. We buy houses in Wasatch County as-is, so a tax balance does not stop us from making an offer.
